paras: The threatened lynching of James Taylor took place in New Rochelle, New York, on July 14, 1903, when a crowd surrounded Taylor, a Black assistant to the city poundkeeper, after he shot a fox terrier, and shouted "Lynch him." A policeman arrested Taylor, who was fined $3 and held for trial on a charge of cruelty to animals. The New York Evening World carried the only known report, as a comic item under the headline "Wanted to Lynch the Dog-Catcher."

Taylor worked for Peel, New Rochelle's poundkeeper and marshal, driving a latticed cart and catching stray dogs with a copper wire. According to the Evening World, he had begun carrying a shotgun in the preceding weeks, and residents of the Hill and Residence Park asserted that he would rather take a dog "dead than alive" to collect his fee.

On July 14 Taylor was seen firing at a fox terrier, and the shot took off one of the dog's legs. Within minutes a crowd of unstated size surrounded him, shouting "Lynch him"; the paper said the cry came "in the most approved Delaware tones." No violence against Taylor is reported, and a policeman who was called to the scene arrested him.

In court Taylor said he had first caught the dog with a wire and fired only after it escaped. He was fined $3 for discharging a shotgun, after which Harry Stiles, described as "a prominent young man of New Rochelle," charged him with cruelty to animals, a case to be prosecuted by Officer O'Brien of the S.P.C.A. No report of the outcome of that prosecution, or of any action against the crowd, was found.

The Evening World's article was written in a joking register aimed at New Rochelle's "colony" of artists, actors and millionaires, and its sympathy lay with the pet owners. It referred to Taylor repeatedly as "the negro," quipped that he "may possibly become the man behind the bars," and mentioned the lynching cry without comment beyond the Delaware comparison. No other white paper and no Black paper is known to have reported the incident.

accounts.label: Residents' complaints as reported by the Evening World
accounts.gist: Residents asserted that Taylor preferred to take dogs dead rather than alive to earn his fee, and that pets had been killed or maimed across the city for weeks.

accounts.label: Taylor's defense in court
accounts.gist: Taylor said he had first caught the dog with a wire, it escaped, and he then shot at it.

framing.detail: The Evening World treated the episode as comedy at New Rochelle's expense ('allied trades of art, literature and money'), sided with the pet owners against Taylor, and reported the 'Lynch him' cry without condemnation, likening it to 'Delaware tones'.

sources.note: Only report: crowd shouted 'Lynch him' at James Taylor, Black assistant to New Rochelle's poundkeeper, after he shot a fox terrier; arrested, fined $3, held on cruelty charge.
quotes: in a few minutes the negro with his gun was surrounded by a crowd who shouted "Lynch him" in the most approved Delaware tones.
The negro's defense was that he had first caught the dog with a wire and that after that it escaped from him, and so he took a shot at it.
Taylor is the man behind the gun and may possibly become the man behind the bars.
